questions.question: What did this actually cost end to end, in dollars and in your own hours, once you count everything beyond the $9 labeling spend buried in the backup slide?
questions.why: The cost slide is marked Q&A-only and mostly says 'subscription' and 'my estimate,' which isn't enough for someone who has to justify spend to a boss.

questions.question: With forty-five or more forks possible for one bug, who or what decides which experiments actually get run first?
questions.why: The fork-tree slide shows a huge branching space but never explains the prioritization rule for picking among that many options.

questions.question: This all seems to run through one person as coordinator, reviewer, and the one who flips production — how does a team of several people actually adopt this without becoming a bottleneck?
questions.why: Every gate and orchestration step described funnels back to a single senior session and 'my own hands,' which doesn't obviously translate to a team.

questions.question: Is two in three good enough to ship to real users, and what's the number you're targeting before you'd call this done?
questions.why: The lot-level accuracy of 65.2% is presented as 'not done, but measurable' without stating what threshold would be acceptable.

questions.question: An idle tab burned a full day's API allowance before anyone noticed — what actually caught that, and how fast would a real cost overrun get flagged now?
questions.why: The watchdog is described as coming after the incident, which raises the question of what monitoring exists going forward.

questions.question: The persona panel said DONE but the real app was unusable the next morning — what changed in the gate after that, or could it fail silently again?
questions.why: The talk shows the gate failing outright and calls hands-on review 'necessary' without saying how the panel itself was fixed.

questions.question: If a PM on my team doesn't run git worktrees or write gate code themselves, what's the actual first thing they'd do on Monday?
questions.why: The two 'next week' asks are written for someone who can already set up experiments, not for a non-engineer deciding whether to greenlight this.

questions.question: Who has the authority to make the calls you kept for yourself, like flipping something to production, once this isn't a one-person project anymore?
questions.why: Gates and flags slide explicitly reserves the production call for the speaker alone, which is a governance question for any team-scale version.

questions.question: What's actually in the starter kit — does it assume the same subscription and tooling you had, or does it work with a normal team stack?
questions.why: The starter kit is name-dropped once at the end with no detail on what it requires to use.

questions.question: When an unattended overnight run picks the wrong fork, what's the blast radius before a human notices and how do you roll it back?
questions.why: The talk emphasizes gates catching bad results but doesn't say what happens when a gate itself is wrong, beyond the persona-review miss.
